scenes.narration: Traceability links four things for every procedure. The scope, say scope seven, used on patient forty-four seventy-one. The reprocessing cycle, cycle eleven forty-two, which passed. And the operator, technician twelve. With that chain, a suspected transmission can be traced to exactly who was exposed.

scenes.narration: Around that chain sit four more safeguards. Microbiological surveillance of scopes at defined intervals, with defined actions on a positive result. Reprocessor validation, including final rinse water quality. Records of every cycle. And a damage and repair log, since a scope back from repair is reprocessed before use.

scenes.narration: If transmission is suspected, first quarantine the scope. Don't reprocess it: that destroys the evidence. Notify infection control and microbiology. Retrieve the records of every exposed patient. Review practice, and sample the scope and reprocessor. Check its repair history. Then consider patient notification, report externally where required, and write it up.

scenes.narration: Most of these failures share one cause: time pressure. When a list runs late and one scope is available, a technician decides alone whether brushing was adequate. That decision shouldn't rest on individual courage. It needs written policy, a defined right to hold a scope back, adequate inventory and staffing, and recorded deviations.
